title: The riddle threat: fourth or seventh day?
summary: The KJV places the threat to Samson’s wife on day seven; Brenton’s English Septuagint translation places it on day four. Their descriptions of the answer’s time also differ.
text: Both editions give a seven-day riddle deadline and an answer on day seven. At 14:15 the KJV dates the threat to the seventh day; Brenton prints the fourth. At 14:18 the KJV has the answer before sunset, whereas Brenton prints before sunrise. Original-language wording: at 14:15 the KJV has “on the seventh day” and the Hebrew (WLC) בַּיֹּ֣ום הַשְּׁבִיעִ֗י [on the seventh day]; the Brenton Greek has ἐν τῇ ἡμέρᾳ τῇ τετάρτῃ [on the fourth day]. At 14:18 the KJV has “before the sun went down” and the Hebrew בְּטֶ֙רֶם֙ יָבֹ֣א הַחַ֔רְסָה [before the sun went in]; the Greek has πρὸ τοῦ ἀνατεῖλαι τὸν ἥλιον [before the sun rose]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/7/14/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/JDG14.htm.
reasoning: The threat date is a direct difference in the same episode, not merely a differently sized participant list. The sunrise and sunset phrases also differ, although before-sunset wording alone does not exclude an earlier morning answer. The seven-day weeping statement can be a narrative recap; the order of adjacent sentences need not prove all pressure began only after the threat.
scope: Brenton is an English translation of a Septuagint text, not a critical Greek apparatus. These observations do not establish every Greek witness, an original reading or an actual historical timetable. Do not treat the KJV’s seventh-day threat and seven-day weeping as an unavoidable internal contradiction; earlier pressure or a recap remains possible. The fourth-day and sunrise readings are now confirmed in the Greek edition itself, not only in Brenton’s English. title: Samson’s third answer: a sentence the KJV does not finish
summary: In the KJV, Samson’s third answer to Delilah stops at “with the web”, and he then wakes without having been said to sleep. The Septuagint has the rest: the result he promises, his sleep, and Delilah weaving his hair.
text: KJV Judges 16:13–14: “If thou weavest the seven locks of my head with the web.” “And she fastened it with the pin” … “And he awaked out of his sleep”. The Hebrew (WLC) is as short: אִם־תַּאַרְגִ֗י אֶת־שֶׁ֛בַע מַחְלְפֹ֥ות רֹאשִׁ֖י עִם־הַמַּסָּֽכֶת then וַתִּתְקַע֙ בַּיָּתֵ֔ד [and she fastened with the pin]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek), 16:13: ἐὰν ὑφάνῃς τὰς ἑπτὰ σειρὰς τῆς κεφαλῆς μου σὺν τῷ διάσματι, καὶ ἐγκρούσῃς τῷ πασσάλῳ εἰς τὸν τοῖχον, καὶ ἔσομαι ὡς εἷς τῶν ἀνθρώπων ἀσθενής [if you weave the seven locks of my head with the web, and drive the pin into the wall, I shall be weak like one of the men]; 16:14: Καὶ ἐγένετο ἐν τῷ κοιμᾶσθαι αὐτὸν, καὶ ἔλαβε Δαλιδὰ τὰς ἑπτὰ σειρὰς τῆς κεφαλῆς αὐτοῦ, καὶ ὕφανεν ἐν τῷ διάσματι [and while he slept Delilah took the seven locks of his head and wove them in the web]. The first two answers in the KJV end with the result: “then shall I be weak, and be as another man” (16:7; 16:11). Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/7/16/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/JDG16.htm.
reasoning: The Greek carries a clause and a half that the Hebrew and KJV lack, and it supplies exactly what the shorter text leaves open: the promised result, the sleep and the weaving. The pattern of the first two answers shows what the third is missing.
scope: This shows a longer text in one Greek edition. It does not show that the Hebrew lost the words in copying or that the Greek added them; both are explanations, not readings. title: Water for Samson: out of the jawbone, or at a place called Lehi?
summary: The KJV has God split a hollow “in the jaw” and then says the spring “is in Lehi unto this day”. The Hebrew uses the same two words both times. The Septuagint has “jaw” both times.
text: KJV Judges 15:19: “God clave an hollow place that was in the jaw” … “which is in Lehi unto this day”. Hebrew (WLC): first אֶת־הַמַּכְתֵּ֣שׁ אֲשֶׁר־בַּלֶּ֗חִי [the hollow that is in lehi], then אֲשֶׁ֣ר בַּלֶּ֔חִי עַ֖ד הַיֹּ֥ום הַזֶּֽה [that is in lehi to this day]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek): τὸν λάκκον τὸν ἐν τῇ σιαγόνι [the hollow in the jaw] … ἥ ἐστιν ἐν σιαγόνι [which is in jaw]. In the KJV, Lehi is the place of the fight (“spread themselves in Lehi”, 15:9), named in 15:17: “called that place Ramathlehi”. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/7/15/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/JDG15.htm.
reasoning: One Hebrew phrase is given two meanings inside one KJV verse. Read the first way, water comes out of the donkey’s jawbone; read the second way, it comes from a hollow in the ground at Lehi, where a spring could still be shown “unto this day”.
scope: The Hebrew word is both the common noun “jaw” and the place name, so the Hebrew does not decide between the two, and the Greek chose “jaw” throughout. The H tag marks only that the KJV’s two renderings cannot both match the one Hebrew phrase; it does not claim which is right. title: The angel’s name: “secret” or “wonderful”?
summary: The KJV has the angel refuse his name because “it is secret”. The Hebrew word is from the root the KJV renders “wonderously” in the next verse, and the Septuagint says “it is wonderful”.
text: KJV Judges 13:18: “Why askest thou thus after my name, seeing it is secret?”. Hebrew (WLC): וְהוּא־פֶֽלִאי [and it is wonderful]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/7/13/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/JDG13.htm.
reasoning: Hebrew and Greek agree on a word of wonder; the KJV gives a word of concealment. In the Hebrew the name’s description and the angel’s act in the next verse echo each other, which the KJV’s “secret” hides.

title: Micah’s graven and molten image
summary: An Israelite household makes “a graven image and a molten image”, the exact pair Deuteronomy 27:15 curses, and dedicates the silver to the LORD. The tribe of Dan then sets the image up. No rebuke or penalty of Micah is narrated; the narrator remarks only that every man did what was right in his own eyes.
text: Law: Exodus 20:4 (KJV) “Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image”; Deuteronomy 27:15 (KJV) “Cursed be the man that maketh any graven or molten image”, Hebrew (WLC) אֲשֶׁ֣ר יַעֲשֶׂה֩ פֶ֨סֶל וּמַסֵּכָ֜ה. Act: Micah is “a man of mount Ephraim” (17:1). Judges 17:3 (KJV): “I had wholly dedicated the silver unto the Lord from my hand for my son, to make a graven image and a molten image”; Hebrew לַֽעֲשֹׂות֙ פֶּ֣סֶל וּמַסֵּכָ֔ה. Judges 17:4: “who made thereof a graven image and a molten image: and they were in the house of Micah”; Hebrew וַֽיַּעֲשֵׂ֙הוּ֙ פֶּ֣סֶל וּמַסֵּכָ֔ה. Judges 17:5: “had an house of gods, and made an ephod, and teraphim, and consecrated one of his sons, who became his priest”. Afterwards: Judges 18:30–31 (KJV) “the children of Dan set up the graven image” … “all the time that the house of God was in Shiloh”. The narrator’s only comment is 17:6: “every man did that which was right in his own eyes”. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/5/27/ and https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/7/17/.
reasoning: The people are Israelites in the land, long after Sinai. The act matches the law word for word in Hebrew: the same verb, “make”, and the same two nouns. Micah is not rebuked or punished in the story; he loses the image to Dan, where it stays in use. A search of the packaged KJV after Judges finds no later mention of Micah’s image; 2 Kings 10:29 condemns the golden calves at Dan, a different object made by Jeroboam.
scope: Not tagged V: the owner ruled on 2026-10-12 that the narrator’s remark at 17:6 counts as a check on the whole episode, so the act is not clearly unchecked. No rebuke in the passage is not proof of no rebuke anywhere in the Bible: the later-book check was a word search of the packaged KJV, not a reading of every book. General condemnations of idols in the prophets do not name this act. Deuteronomy 27:15 adds “and putteth it in a secret place”, which a household shrine may or may not fit. title: The priest of Dan: grandson of Manasseh, or of Moses?
summary: The KJV calls Dan’s idol-priest “Jonathan, the son of Gershom, the son of Manasseh”. In the Leningrad Codex one letter of “Manasseh” is written as a suspended letter; without it the name is “Moses”, whose son was Gershom.
text: KJV Judges 18:30: “Jonathan, the son of Gershom, the son of Manasseh, he and his sons were priests to the tribe of Dan”. Hebrew (WLC): וִ֠יהֹונָתָן בֶּן־גֵּרְשֹׁ֨ם בֶּן־מְנַשֶּׁ֜ה. The Unicode/XML Leningrad Codex edition prints the last name as מְנַ[7]שֶּׁ֜ה, and its key defines note 7 as “Suspended letter(s). Shown as suspended letters.” The marked letter is the n; the remaining consonants, m-sh-h, are the consonants of “Moses”. The Brenton Greek reads Manasseh: Ἰωνάθαν υἱὸς Γηρσὼν υἱὸς Μανασσῆ. Elsewhere in the KJV, Gershom is Moses’ son: Exodus 2:22 “he called his name Gershom”; 1 Chronicles 23:15 “The sons of Moses were, Gershom, and Eliezer”; 1 Chronicles 26:24 “Shebuel the son of Gershom, the son of Moses”. The priest is introduced as a Levite (Judges 17:7, “who was a Levite”); Moses was of the house of Levi (Exodus 2:1), and Manasseh was not a Levite tribe. Fetched from https://tanach.us/Server.txt?Judg18:30-18:30, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/7/18/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/JDG18.htm.
reasoning: The codex itself sets one letter apart, and that letter is the only difference between the two names. A Levite named as son of Gershom fits Moses’ line as given in Exodus and Chronicles and does not fit Manasseh’s. If “Moses” is read, the first priest of Dan’s graven image is Moses’ grandson.
scope: Reading “Moses” is an inference from the scribal marking, not what the codex’s vowels say: as pointed, the word is Manasseh, which the KJV and this Greek edition follow. The consonantal Aleppo-based edition served by bolls.life prints the name with no marking. Why the letter is suspended is not stated in the text, and a different, otherwise unknown Gershom is not excluded. The statement about the codex rests on one edition’s transcription note. title: Where Israel asked God: “the house of God” or Bethel?
summary: Four times the KJV says Israel went to “the house of God”. The Hebrew has the place name Bethel each time, and so does the Septuagint. In the KJV the ark seems to be at the sanctuary; in the Hebrew and Greek it is at Bethel.
text: KJV Judges 20:18: “went up to the house of God, and asked counsel of God”; 20:26: “came unto the house of God, and wept”; 20:31: “of which one goeth up to the house of God”; 21:2: “the people came to the house of God”. Hebrew (WLC): 20:18 וַיַּעֲל֣וּ בֵֽית־אֵל֮ [and went up to Bethel]; 20:26 וַיָּבֹ֣אוּ בֵֽית־אֵ֗ל; 20:31 עֹלָ֣ה בֵֽית־אֵ֗ל; 21:2 וַיָּבֹ֤א הָעָם֙ בֵּֽית־אֵ֔ל. Septuagint (Brenton Greek): 20:18 ἀνέβησαν εἰς Βαιθὴλ; 20:26 ἦλθον εἰς Βαιθήλ; 20:31 ἀναβαίνουσα εἰς Βαιθὴλ; 21:2 ἦλθεν ὁ λαὸς εἰς Βαιθὴλ. KJV 20:27: “the ark of the covenant of God was there in those days”. Where the KJV has “house of God” at 18:31 (“the house of God was in Shiloh”), the Hebrew phrase is a different one: בֵּית־הָאֱלֹהִ֖ים בְּשִׁלֹֽה. The KJV itself prints “Bethel” at 21:19. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/7/20/, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/7/21/, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/7/18/, https://ebible.org/grcbrent/JDG20.htm and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/JDG21.htm.
reasoning: Hebrew and Greek name a town; the KJV turns the name into a description that a reader will connect with the sanctuary just located at Shiloh (18:31). On the Hebrew and Greek wording, the ark and the sacrifices of 20:26–27 are at Bethel, not Shiloh.
scope: The name Bethel is made of the words “house” and “God”, so the KJV’s rendering is a possible reading of the two words; the case against it is the Greek, the different Hebrew phrase at 18:31 and the KJV’s own “Bethel” at 21:19. A shared root does not settle context. The verses do not say why the ark was at Bethel or for how long, and no unauthorised-sanctuary claim is made. title: Benjamin’s army: mustered, killed and escaped
summary: Benjamin musters 26,700. The dead are given as 25,100 and then as 25,000, and 600 escape. That leaves about 1,000 men unaccounted for. The Septuagint musters 23,000, fewer than the dead and escaped together.
text: KJV Judges 20:15: “twenty and six thousand men that drew sword, beside the inhabitants of Gibeah, which were numbered seven hundred chosen men” (26,700). 20:35: “twenty and five thousand and an hundred men”. 20:44–45: “eighteen thousand men”, “five thousand men”, “two thousand men”; 20:46: “twenty and five thousand men that drew the sword”. 20:47: “six hundred men turned and fled”. 25,100 + 600 = 25,700; 25,000 + 600 = 25,600; the muster is 26,700. The Hebrew (WLC) has the KJV’s figures: 20:15 עֶשְׂרִ֨ים וְשִׁשָּׁ֥ה אֶ֛לֶף [twenty-six thousand]; 20:35 עֶשְׂרִ֨ים וַחֲמִשָּׁ֥ה אֶ֛לֶף וּמֵאָ֖ה אִ֑ישׁ; 20:47 שֵׁ֥שׁ מֵאֹ֖ות אִ֑ישׁ. The Brenton Greek at 20:15 has εἰκοσιτρεῖς χιλιάδες [twenty-three thousand] with the same seven hundred (ἑπτακόσιοι ἄνδρες), 25,100 at 20:35 (εἴκοσι καὶ πέντε χιλιάδας καὶ ἑκατὸν ἄνδρας) and six hundred at 20:47 (ἑξακόσιοι ἄνδρες): a muster of 23,700 against 25,700 dead and escaped. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/7/20/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/JDG20.htm.
reasoning: These are figures for one army in one chapter. In the KJV and Hebrew about a thousand men are neither killed nor among the survivors, and the day’s dead are stated two ways, 25,100 and 25,000. In the Greek edition the dead and the escaped outnumber the men mustered by two thousand.
scope: Benjamin’s own losses on the first two days are not stated (20:21 and 20:25 give only Israel’s), so a thousand earlier deaths would close the KJV gap; that is a supplied figure, not a stated one. 25,000 may be 25,100 rounded. 20:48 adds further killing in the towns without a number.
